text: Metrics and logs are things you have to go look at — someone opens Metrics Explorer, someone writes a KQL query. An alert rule flips that around entirely: it watches on your behalf, continuously, and does something the moment a condition becomes true. Every alert rule boils down to the same two halves: a condition, what to watch for, and an action, what happens the instant it's true.

A condition names a signal — a metric or a log query — a threshold, and how often it's checked. Average CPU, checked every minute, over 80% for the last 5 minutes — fire. That 5-minute evaluation window isn't decoration: without it, one normal 2-second CPU spike would trigger a noisy, useless alert, which is exactly what this window exists to prevent.

An Action Group is a separate, reusable object defining what happens when any alert fires: email, SMS, a webhook, an Azure Function, a Logic App, an automation runbook. Define it once, then attach it to as many alert rules as you want — a CPU alert here, a disk-space alert there, even next lesson's budget alert, all notifying the team the same consistent way.

A complete alert rule has four parts: scope, which resource or resources it watches; the condition from before; an Action Group to run; and a severity, Sev 0 (most critical) through Sev 4 (least). Severity doesn't change what fires — it just helps whoever's on call triage a flood of alerts by how serious each one actually is, instead of treating every notification the same.

A VM's CPU alert — condition: average CPU over 80% for 5 minutes, scope: that one VM — fires. Its Action Group emails the infrastructure team and calls an Azure Function that resizes the VM automatically. No one had to be watching. Next up: the other thing worth alerting on entirely — cost — and the budgets that catch a runaway bill before it ever arrives.
